tldr: By building two coupled world models (C-JEPA and W-JEPA) that predict both robot dynamics and wireless channel conditions in latent space, the authors show that a remote robot can navigate autonomously with resilience while cutting transmission power, even under unstable communication.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed coupled control and wireless world model framework. On the edge server, C-JEPA predicts robot actions and visual states while W-JEPA forecasts radio channel conditions and future transmit power. Together, they maintain remote control while pruning unnecessary transmissions.
overview:
When remotely controlling robots in factories or warehouses over wireless links, engineers hit a major wall. Streaming rich video like camera feeds continuously over the uplink congests bandwidth and quickly drains batteries. On top of that, signal blockage, interference, and packet loss are everyday realities in these environments.

To tackle this, the authors asked: could we drastically cut communication by jointly forecasting both robot motion and radio wave behavior ahead of time? Specifically, they propose a framework based on the self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), coupling a control model (C-JEPA) and a wireless model (W-JEPA) in latent space. The system anticipates where the robot will move next and whether wireless conditions will be good or bad, scheduling image transmissions intermittently only when channel quality is high.

For validation, they built a simulation platform fully synchronizing Gazebo (a physics engine for robotics) and Sionna (a ray-tracing tool for realistic radio propagation) via ROS. They evaluated the system under harsh conditions, including carrier frequency shifts, multipath from obstacles, access point handovers, sudden connection outages, and lighting changes.

The results show that compared to conventional Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and PID control, the approach cuts uplink transmission energy by more than half (down to 4.74 J) while reducing lap times. It also demonstrates remarkable resilience, sustaining autonomous navigation even across 13 consecutive dropped transmission steps without failing.
contributions: Built a practical simulation testbed synchronizing a robot physics simulator (Gazebo) and high-fidelity radio ray-tracing (Sionna) via ROS to jointly evaluate communication and control

Developed a communication-aware framework that couples vision-based control prediction (C-JEPA) and wireless channel prediction (W-JEPA) in latent space to prune transmissions while maintaining remote control
Demonstrated a transfer learning strategy to efficiently adapt a world model pretrained in a lightweight reinforcement learning environment (Gym) to the Gazebo environment
Extracted structured RF representations from Channel State Information (CSI), including spectrograms and Persistence Images (PIs), significantly improving channel prediction accuracy

Proposed an adaptive resilience mechanism that detects visual disturbances like lighting changes or lens occlusions from latent prediction discrepancies, self-healing without retraining the control policy

sections.heading: How do you remotely control a robot when connections keep dropping?
sections.summary: In next-generation remote robot control, the overhead of streaming high-dimensional sensor data and unreliable wireless connectivity are major bottlenecks. This paper proposes a multimodal world model that forecasts both control dynamics and wireless channels to achieve stable control under severe radio conditions.
sections.details:
Demand for remote robot control is booming in warehouse automation, plant inspection, and disaster response. However, constantly streaming heavy data like camera images to a base station in real time strains network bandwidth and spikes the robot's power consumption. In real-world industrial sites, radio blockage from obstacles, multipath reflections, and packet losses happen all the time.

To address this, world models—internal models that predict environmental dynamics—have recently drawn strong attention. However, conventional world models focus almost solely on the physical motion of the robot, largely ignoring whether the wireless channel is good or bad.

Here lies the key insight: attempting to transmit images when the radio channel is poor leads to dropped packets and wasted energy. Conversely, if the system can forecast when the channel will improve or how long the robot can safely move without new images, it can intelligently prune (schedule) communications. Expanding on prior ideas, the authors integrated the Gazebo robotics simulator with the Sionna radio propagation simulator, proposing a robust system capable of withstanding realistic disturbances and channel perturbations.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of world models, joint communication-control, and simulation
sections.summary: This section reviews three research trends—latent-space prediction without pixel reconstruction (JEPA), communication-aware control co-optimizing wireless and control resources, and high-fidelity simulator integration—and explains how this work bridges the gaps between them.
sections.details:
This work stands at the intersection of three main research areas:

- World Models and JEPA: Traditional world models mostly reconstructed future camera images pixel by pixel, which is computationally expensive and prone to distraction from irrelevant background noise. Recently, the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) emerged to predict future states purely within latent embedding spaces. This work introduces JEPA into both control and wireless domains.
- Communication-Aware Robotic Control: Past work primarily focused on stabilizing control over a given, fixed communication channel. Recent studies have shifted toward controllers that actively optimize communication resources and transmission timings. However, simultaneously modeling the latent dynamics of both communication and control in realistic robotic setups has remained extremely rare.
- Integrated Robot-Wireless Simulation: While Gazebo is a de facto standard in robotics and Sionna is a benchmark ray-tracing tool in wireless communications, no prior research has coupled them to rigorously simulate how robot motion alters radio propagation, and how deteriorating channels feed back into robot control.

sections.heading: Two synchronized engines: coupled JEPA and adaptive architecture
sections.summary: A detailed look at the mathematical formulations of vision-oriented C-JEPA and radio-oriented W-JEPA, topological RF representations, an online adaptation mechanism for visual disturbances, and the implementation pipeline linking Gazebo and Sionna.
sections.details:
### III-A Joint C-JEPA and W-JEPA Learning
The overall system consists of the robot and a remote controller located at the access point (AP). The robot sends camera observations $\boldsymbol{o}_t$ via uplink and receives control actions $a_t$ via downlink.

Two models run on the controller side. First, the control-oriented C-JEPA consists of an image encoder $\mathcal{E}_{\phi_c}^c$ and a Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM), which captures memory and uncertainty via deterministic states $h_t$ and stochastic states $z_t$. It predicts future latent states with a prior distribution $p_{\phi_c}$ from past actions and states, trained by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence against the posterior distribution $q_{\phi_c}$ obtained from actual observations. A reward predictor $\mathcal{D}_r^c$ and a continuation predictor $\mathcal{D}_\tau^c$ are trained jointly, and the policy $\pi_{\theta_c}$ outputs control actions.

Meanwhile, the wireless-oriented W-JEPA maps received wireless observations $q_t$ into latent representations $c_t$ using an encoder $\mathcal{E}_{\phi_w}^w$. A wireless predictor $\mathcal{P}_{\phi_w}^w$ then forecasts future radio states $\hat{c}_t$, taking as input not only the previous wireless state $c_{t-1}$ but also the robot's latent state $(h_t, z_t)$ predicted by C-JEPA. Where the robot moves directly dictates future channel conditions. From this prediction, future transmit power $\hat{p}_t$ is estimated. When conditions are predicted to be favorable, a binary scheduling variable is set to $\rho_t=1$ to request image transmission; when conditions are poor, $\rho_t=0$ skips transmission.

### III-B Structured RF Representations for W-JEPA
Instead of relying solely on Raw CSI (amplitude and phase across subcarriers), the authors introduce two structured RF representations to better capture temporal variations. The first is a spectrogram image $q_t^s$ obtained via short-time Fourier transform over sliding windows. The second is a Persistence Image (PI) $q_t^p$ based on persistent homology from topological data analysis (TDA). By constructing point clouds via time-delay embeddings and mapping the birth and death of topological holes into images, periodic multipath structures are reliably captured.

### III-C Adaptive Resilience Mechanism
During operation, global degradations (such as dim or reddish lighting) or local occlusions (such as mud splatters on the lens) cause a discrepancy $\Delta_t$ between C-JEPA's predicted latent variable $\hat{z}$ and the actual observed latent variable $z$. If this divergence exceeds a threshold $\delta$, an anomaly is flagged. For global illumination shifts, the system quickly evaluates pre-configured HSV color transformation parameters and selects the one that minimizes the discrepancy. For local occlusions, a lightweight Variational Autoencoder (VAE) adapts online using past buffered images to reconstruct the missing regions. The crucial advantage is instant recovery at the perception front-end without retraining the control policy itself.

### III-D & III-E Sionna–Gazebo Integration & Experimental Setup
In the simulation pipeline, 3D scenes from Gazebo (SDF format) are assigned radio material properties (conforming to ITU recommendations) in Blender and converted to Mitsuba XML format for Sionna. The Waveshare JetBot's pose is streamed via ROS to Sionna at millisecond resolution, enabling accurate, on-the-fly radio propagation ray-tracing.

### III-F Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation
Training reinforcement learning from scratch inside Gazebo is computationally heavy. Therefore, C-JEPA is pretrained in the lightweight 2D Gym CarRacing environment and then transferred to Gazebo's visual inputs and reward scheme. Five discrete actions are mapped into continuous linear and angular velocity commands for the JetBot, yielding smooth navigation.

sections.heading: Experimental results: slashing communication while navigating severe disruptions
sections.summary: The method was evaluated across eight scenarios, covering nominal navigation (E1), drastic radio channel shifts (E2–E4), RF representation comparisons (E5), sustained connection loss (E6), and visual disturbances (E7–E8). The proposed approach sharply reduced energy and latency while achieving superior completion rates under stress.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Experimental Scenarios and Baselines
Evaluations covered eight scenarios: E1 (nominal baseline), E2 (added reflectors and obstacles), E3 (access point handover), E4 (carrier frequency shifts from 2.14 GHz to 1.9 GHz and 2.6 GHz), E5 (RF representation comparison), E6 (consecutive packet loss resilience), and E7–E8 (visual perturbations). Baselines included a Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained under the same transfer protocol and a classic PID controller.

### IV-C Overall Performance and Robustness
In the nominal scenario (E1), the proposed method achieved a lap time of 57.1 s and an average cumulative reward of 775.4, outperforming DQN (58.0 s, 753.8 reward) and PID (77.3 s, 716.1 reward). Communication efficiency stood out: while DQN consumed 9.21 J and PID consumed 11.19 J in uplink transmission energy, the proposed method needed only 4.74 J—more than a 50% reduction—by transmitting only when necessary. Uplink latency was also lowest at 0.48 ms.

Robustness against disturbances was equally striking. Lap times barely fluctuated under frequency changes (E4) or additional reflectors (E2). When subjected to forced access point handovers during navigation (E3), DQN and PID completion rates crashed to 56.48% and 58.99%, respectively, due to collisions. In contrast, the proposed method maintained a 100% completion rate.

### IV-D Comparison of Structured RF Representations
Comparing W-JEPA inputs in E5 revealed that spectrograms and Persistence Images (PIs) maintained lower power prediction errors over longer time horizons $H$ than Raw CSI. PIs achieved the lowest error overall. However, feature extraction took 0 ms for Raw CSI, 0.58 ms for spectrograms, and 13.56 ms for PIs. This outlines a clear trade-off: PIs for maximum accuracy, spectrograms for a balanced trade-off with real-time speed, and Raw CSI when computational resources are severely constrained.

### IV-E Communication Efficiency and Packet Loss Tolerance
The 400-dimensional C-JEPA latent embedding requires roughly 62 times less data than the token size ($128 \times 196$) needed for comparable Vision Transformer (ViT) approaches. Furthermore, under consecutive uplink dropouts (E6), the ViT baseline failed after about 8 steps. In contrast, the proposed method's internal world model maintained forward rollouts autonomously, keeping the robot on course for up to 13 consecutive dropped steps (~0.45 s) without crashing.

### IV-F Adaptation to Visual Perturbations
Sudden lighting shifts (E7) caused unadapted controllers to fail, but online HSV parameter switching promptly restored tracking and preserved high rewards. Under localized occlusions such as mud splatters (E8), online inpainting via the lightweight VAE similarly allowed the robot to complete navigation smoothly.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: moving to physical robots and multi-agent fleets
sections.summary: Coupled control-wireless JEPAs significantly improve communication efficiency, robustness, and fault tolerance in remote robotics. Future directions aim to transition from single-robot simulation to multi-robot collaboration, real-world deployments, and full digital twin architectures.
sections.details:
This work introduced a communication-aware remote control framework that couples robot motion dynamics and wireless channel evolution within a shared latent predictive space. Leveraging structured RF representations for channel forecasting and a zero-policy-retraining adaptation mechanism for visual disturbances, the system maintains robust control even in severely bandwidth-constrained and volatile environments. Processing speeds were also verified to run in real time on a single GPU.

Looking ahead, the current setup is limited to a single robot over an isolated wireless link. Expanding this to multi-agent environments where multiple robots compete for shared spectrum is an important next step. In addition, because evaluation is currently restricted to simulation (Gazebo + Sionna), future work will focus on physical experiments with JetBots over real private 5G and Wi-Fi networks, progressing toward fully synchronized physical-to-virtual digital twin platforms.

takeaways: Robot motion and radio channel dynamics are tightly correlated; coupling both world models in latent space lets the system intelligently prune unnecessary transmissions.
Converting raw CSI into structured representations like spectrograms or Persistence Images (PIs) substantially enhances long-horizon wireless channel forecasting.
Monitoring discrepancies in latent space allows perception front-ends (via color adjustments or VAE inpainting) to rapidly recover from disturbances without retraining policy weights.
Coupling Gazebo and Sionna via ROS provides a powerful, realistic simulation testbed for research at the intersection of wireless communications and robotics.
limitations: Evaluations are currently limited to Gazebo and Sionna simulations, leaving physical hardware characteristics and complex real-world RF interference unverified.
The setup only considers communication between a single robot and a single access point, without handling bandwidth contention in multi-robot environments.
While highly accurate, generating structured RF representations like Persistence Images (PIs) takes around 13.5 ms, posing computational challenges for ultra-high-frequency control loops.
